texts.full_text: st year?—that doesn’t mean you should respond by being upset with him, say experts. “We can’t assume we don’t owe guys an explanation about what that means to us,” says Brandy Engler, author of The Women on My Couch. Why? It's generally assumed that you would take his last name, based on tradition, so it's understandable that he may be confused if it's not your thing. She adds that anyone you’re seriously considering marrying deserves to be part of a conversation about what your last name means to you. After all, if (or when) you tie the knot, you’ll be entering into a partnership in which you’ll be making lots of big decisions together. “This is a common problem in marriages in general,” Engler says. “A person makes a unilateral decision and assumes the other person probably gets it, but they don’t. And then a lot of times, when people don’t have a clear answer on things, the knee-jerk reaction is to take something personally and think something’s wrong with you. It’s just a common human experience.” Greer agrees: “I would encourage a woman to bring it up and say, ‘This is really more about my own self-expression and not about the way that I feel toward you,’” she says. In addition to explaining what’s going through your head, you should also ask what’s going through his. “The conversation would look like, ‘I’m considering keeping my own last name, here’s why, but I wanted to check in with you and ask what it would mean to you if I did that,’” Engler says. “Both people should start speaking their truth.” Then, once the two of you have expressed your needs, you can figure out ways to address them—ways that may or may not look like the ones you two originally envisioned. “That’s what it looks like when you’re not just making decisions for yourself,” Engler says. "Taking the name isn’t usually a deal-breaker for most couples, but it probably is one of those first big decisions, and you want to start the practice of making decisions together." OPINION PER CURIAM: Ray Wallace Mettetal Jr., a/k/a Steven Ray Maupin (the "Defendant"), appeals his conviction for conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute marijuana in violation of 21 U.S.C.A. § 846 and possession with intent to distribute marijuana, also in violation of 21 U.S.C.A. § 841(a)(1). The Defendant was sentenced to a term of imprisonment of eight years followed by five years supervised release. On appeal, the Defendant contends that he received ineffective assistance from his trial counsel because: (i) defense counsel failed to call witnesses; and (ii) defense counsel allowed the Government's expert witness to testify despite an objection. texts.full_text: a challenging future. More than 3 decades ago, it became evident that bone-resorbing osteoclasts are of hematopoietic origin and are ultimately linked to the "basic multicellular unit," where they team up with the other cell types, including bone-forming osteoblasts. Since 2 decades, we have learned about the signaling pathways controlling genes relevant for osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption. It took another decade until the hypothesized "osteoclast differentiation" factor was discovered and was translated into an actional receptor as well in vitro experiments pinpointing how it worked within cells to promote development of mature, functional osteoclasts from precursor hematopoietic stem cell progenitors. This led to defining the role of RANK/RANKL/OPG signaling—a pivotal discovery that provided insights into not just bone physiology but also various pathological conditions associated with skeletal diseases. Research in recent years has focused on identifying additional molecules and pathways involved in osteoclast differentiation, activation, and function beyond traditional RANK-RANK Ligand (RANKL) axis. These include c-Fos signaling crucial for the fusion of mononuclear precursors into multinucleated mature cells capable of resorbing bone matrix efficiently. The nuanced regulation by cytokines like M-CSF and various intracellular kinases also constitutes a significant area under investigation, expanding our understanding beyond single-gene or receptor-mediated pathways. Intriguingly, studies on the cellular microenvironment—how osteoclasts interact with their extracellular milieu—are elucidating mechanisms that can affect resorption efficiency. Looking forward, advancements in molecular biology and genetics hold promise for targeted therapies aimed at controlling excessive bone loss associated with diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or Paget's disease. This promises not only to address the symptoms but potentially alter disease trajectories through early intervention targeting osteoclasts specifically rather than broadly affecting all hematopoietic cells. As research continues, an exciting frontier lies in combining gene therapy approaches and nanotechnology for precise delivery of therapeutic agents directly at sites where bone resorption is undesirably elevated. texts.full_text: hn W. Hirons (1876 – after 1905) was an English footballer who played in the Football League for Small Heath. Hirons was born in the Erdington district of Birmingham.
